formatted_response:
Content from https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis:

Title: Photosynthesis

URL Source: https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis

Published Time: 2001-11-02T21:22:29Z

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Photosynthesis_en.svg/500px-Photosynthesis_en.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Photosynthesis_en.svg)

Schematic of photosynthesis in plants. The [carbohydrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate "Carbohydrate") produced are stored in or used by the plant.

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Seawifs_global_biosphere.jpg/500px-Seawifs_global_biosphere.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seawifs_global_biosphere.jpg)

Composite image showing the global distribution of photosynthesis, including both oceanic [phytoplankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoplankton "Phytoplankton") and terrestrial [vegetation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetation "Vegetation"). Dark red and blue-green indicate regions of high photosynthetic activity in the ocean and on land, respectively.

**Photosynthesis**[[note 1]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-2) is a [system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_system "Biological system") of [biological processes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_process "Biological process") by which [photopigment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photopigment "Photopigment")-bearing [autotrophic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autotroph "Autotroph")[organisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organism "Organism"), such as most [plants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant "Plant"), [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae "Algae") and [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria"), convert [light energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_energy "Light energy")—typically from [sunlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight "Sunlight")—into the [chemical energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_energy "Chemical energy") necessary to fuel their [metabolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolism "Metabolism"). The term _photosynthesis_ usually refers to **oxygenic photosynthesis**, a process that releases [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen") as a [byproduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byproduct "Byproduct") of [water splitting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_splitting "Water splitting"). Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the [bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_bond "Chemical bond") of intracellular [organic compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_compound "Organic compound") (complex [compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_compound "Chemical compound") containing [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon")), typically [carbohydrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate "Carbohydrate") like [sugars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar "Sugar") (mainly [glucose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucose "Glucose"), [fructose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fructose "Fructose") and [sucrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucrose "Sucrose")), [starches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starch "Starch"), [phytoglycogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoglycogen "Phytoglycogen") and [cellulose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellulose "Cellulose"). When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through [cellular respiration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellular_respiration "Cellular respiration"). Photosynthesis plays a critical role in producing and maintaining the [oxygen content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_oxygen "Atmospheric oxygen") of the [Earth's atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere"), and it supplies most of the [biological energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_energy "Biological energy") necessary for [complex life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_life "Complex life") on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").[[2]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-Bryant-2006-3)

Some organisms also perform [anoxygenic photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anoxygenic_photosynthesis "Anoxygenic photosynthesis"), which does not produce oxygen. Some [bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteria "Bacteria") (e.g. [purple bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_bacteria "Purple bacteria")) use [bacteriochlorophyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteriochlorophyll "Bacteriochlorophyll") to split [hydrogen sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_sulfide "Hydrogen sulfide") as a [reductant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductant "Reductant") instead of [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water"), releasing [sulfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur "Sulfur") instead of oxygen, which was a dominant form of photosynthesis in the [euxinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euxinic "Euxinic")[Canfield oceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canfield_ocean "Canfield ocean") during the [Boring Billion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boring_Billion "Boring Billion").[[3]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-Canfield1998-4)[[4]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-Javaux2018-5)[Archaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaea "Archaea") such as _[Halobacterium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halobacterium "Halobacterium")_ also perform a type of non-[carbon-fixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fixation "Carbon fixation") anoxygenic photosynthesis, where the simpler photopigment [retinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retinal "Retinal") and its [microbial rhodopsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microbial_rhodopsin "Microbial rhodopsin")[derivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative_(chemistry) "Derivative (chemistry)") are used to absorb green light and produce a proton ([hydron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydron "Hydron")) [gradient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrochemical_gradient "Electrochemical gradient") across the [cell membrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_membrane "Cell membrane"), and the subsequent [ion movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemiosmosis "Chemiosmosis") powers [transmembrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transmembrane_protein "Transmembrane protein")[proton pumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton_pump "Proton pump") to directly synthesize [adenosine triphosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adenosine_triphosphate "Adenosine triphosphate") (ATP), the "energy currency" of cells. Such archaeal photosynthesis might have been the earliest form of photosynthesis that evolved on Earth, as far back as the [Paleoarchean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleoarchean "Paleoarchean"), preceding that of [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria") (see [Purple Earth hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Earth_hypothesis "Purple Earth hypothesis")).[[5]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-6)

While the details may differ between [species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species "Species"), the process always begins when light energy is absorbed by the [reaction centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reaction_center "Reaction center"), proteins that contain [photosynthetic pigments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthetic_pigment "Photosynthetic pigment") or [chromophores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromophore "Chromophore"). In plants, these pigments are [chlorophylls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorophyll "Chlorophyll") (a [porphyrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porphyrin "Porphyrin") derivative that absorbs the red and blue [spectra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_spectrum "Optical spectrum") of light, thus reflecting green) held inside [chloroplasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloroplast "Chloroplast"), abundant in [leaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaf "Leaf") cells. In cyanobacteria, they are embedded in the [plasma membrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_membrane "Plasma membrane"). In these [light-dependent reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-dependent_reaction "Light-dependent reaction"), some energy is used to strip [electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron") from suitable substances, such as water, producing oxygen gas. The [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen") freed by the splitting of water is used in the creation of two important molecules that participate in energetic processes: reduced [nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotinamide_adenine_dinucleotide_phosphate "Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate") (NADPH) and ATP.

In plants, [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae "Algae"), and [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria"), sugars are synthesized by a subsequent sequence of light-independent reactions called the [Calvin cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_cycle "Calvin cycle"). In this process, atmospheric carbon dioxide is incorporated into already existing organic compounds, such as [ribulose bisphosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribulose_bisphosphate "Ribulose bisphosphate") (RuBP).[[6]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-7) Using the ATP and NADPH produced by the light-dependent reactions, the resulting compounds are then [reduced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_reductant "Biological reductant") and removed to form further carbohydrates, such as [glucose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucose "Glucose"). In other bacteria, different mechanisms like the [reverse Krebs cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_Krebs_cycle "Reverse Krebs cycle") are used to achieve the same end.

The first photosynthetic organisms probably [evolved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolved "Evolved") early in the [evolutionary history of life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_history_of_life "Evolutionary history of life") using [reducing agents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reducing_agent "Reducing agent") such as hydrogen or hydrogen sulfide, rather than water, as sources of electrons.[[7]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-8) Cyanobacteria appeared later; the [excess oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_cycle "Oxygen cycle") they produced contributed directly to the [oxygenation of the Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygenation_of_the_Earth "Oxygenation of the Earth"),[[8]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-9) which rendered the evolution of complex life possible. The average rate of energy captured by global photosynthesis is approximately 130 [terawatts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terawatts "Terawatts"),[[9]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-10)[[10]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-12) which is about eight times the total [power consumption of human civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_consumption_of_human_civilization "Power consumption of human civilization").[[12]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-13) Photosynthetic organisms also convert around 100–115 billion [tons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ton "Ton") (91–104 Pg [petagrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orders_of_magnitude_(mass) "Orders of magnitude (mass)"), or billions of metric tons), of carbon into [biomass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomass_(ecology) "Biomass (ecology)") per year.[[13]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-McGraw-Hill-2007-15) Photosynthesis was discovered in 1779 by [Jan Ingenhousz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Ingenhousz "Jan Ingenhousz") who showed that plants need light, not just soil and water.

## Overview

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Simple_photosynthesis_overview.svg/250px-Simple_photosynthesis_overview.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Simple_photosynthesis_overview.svg)

Photosynthesis changes sunlight into chemical energy, splits water to liberate O 2, and fixes CO 2 into sugar.

Most photosynthetic organisms are [photoautotrophs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photoautotroph "Photoautotroph"), which means that they are able to [synthesize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_synthesis "Chemical synthesis") food directly from [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") and [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water") using [energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy "Energy") from light. However, not all organisms use carbon dioxide as a source of carbon atoms to carry out photosynthesis; [photoheterotrophs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photoheterotroph "Photoheterotroph") use organic compounds, rather than carbon dioxide, as a source of carbon.[[2]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-Bryant-2006-3)

In [plants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant "Plant"), [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae "Algae"), and [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria"), photosynthesis releases oxygen. This **oxygenic photosynthesis** is by far the most common type of photosynthesis used by living organisms. Some shade-loving plants (sciophytes) produce such low levels of oxygen during photosynthesis that they use all of it themselves instead of releasing it to the atmosphere.[[15]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-16)

Although there are some differences between oxygenic photosynthesis in plants, algae, and cyanobacteria, the overall process is quite similar in these organisms. There are also many varieties of [anoxygenic photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anoxygenic_photosynthesis "Anoxygenic photosynthesis"), used mostly by bacteria, which consume carbon dioxide but do not release oxygen or which produce elemental sulfur instead of molecular oxygen.[[16]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-18)

Carbon dioxide is converted into sugars in a process called [carbon fixation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fixation "Carbon fixation"); photosynthesis captures energy from sunlight to convert carbon dioxide into [carbohydrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate "Carbohydrate"). Carbon fixation is an [endothermic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endothermic "Endothermic")[redox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redox "Redox") reaction.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about biological consumption of energy from inorganic compounds. For chemical synthesis in molecular nanotechnology, see [Chemosynthesis (nanotechnology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis_(nanotechnology) "Chemosynthesis (nanotechnology)").

[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Venenivibrio.jpg/250px-Venenivibrio.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Venenivibrio.jpg)

_[Venenivibrio stagnispumantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venenivibrio\_stagnispumantis "Venenivibrio stagnispumantis")_ gains energy by oxidizing hydrogen gas.

In biochemistry, **chemosynthesis** is the biological conversion of one or more carbon-containing molecules (usually [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") or [methane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methane "Methane")) and nutrients into organic matter using the [oxidation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation "Oxidation") of inorganic compounds (e.g., [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen") gas, [hydrogen sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_sulfide "Hydrogen sulfide")) or [ferrous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrous "Ferrous") ions as a source of energy, rather than sunlight, as in [photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis "Photosynthesis"). [Chemoautotrophs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemotroph "Chemotroph"), [organisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organism "Organism") that obtain carbon from [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") through chemosynthesis, are phylogenetically diverse. Groups that include conspicuous or biogeochemically important taxa include the sulfur-oxidizing [Gammaproteobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammaproteobacteria "Gammaproteobacteria"), the [Campylobacterota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campylobacterota "Campylobacterota"), the [Aquificota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquificota "Aquificota"), the [methanogenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methanogen "Methanogen") archaea, and the neutrophilic [iron-oxidizing bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron-oxidizing_bacteria "Iron-oxidizing bacteria").

Many microorganisms in dark regions of the oceans use chemosynthesis to produce biomass from single-carbon molecules. Two categories can be distinguished. In the rare sites where hydrogen molecules (H 2) are available, the energy available from the reaction between CO 2 and H 2 (leading to production of methane, CH 4) can be large enough to drive the production of biomass. Alternatively, in most oceanic environments, energy for chemosynthesis derives from reactions in which substances such as [hydrogen sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_sulfide "Hydrogen sulfide") or [ammonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia "Ammonia") are oxidized. This may occur with or without the presence of oxygen.

Many chemosynthetic microorganisms are consumed by other organisms in the ocean, and [symbiotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbiosis "Symbiosis") associations between chemosynthesizers and respiring heterotrophs are quite common. Large populations of animals can be supported by chemosynthetic [secondary production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_production "Secondary production") at [hydrothermal vents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrothermal_vent "Hydrothermal vent"), [methane clathrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methane_clathrate "Methane clathrate"), [cold seeps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_seep "Cold seep"), [whale falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whale_fall "Whale fall"), and [isolated cave water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movile_Cave "Movile Cave").

It has been hypothesized that anaerobic chemosynthesis may support life below the surface of [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_on_Mars "Life on Mars"), [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter")'s moon [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)"), and other planets.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-1) Chemosynthesis may have also been the first type of metabolism that evolved on Earth, leading the way for cellular respiration and photosynthesis to develop later.

## Hydrogen sulfide chemosynthesis process

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chemosynthesis&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Hydrogen sulfide chemosynthesis process")]

[Giant tube worms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_tube_worm "Giant tube worm") use bacteria in their [trophosome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trophosome "Trophosome") to [fix carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fixation "Carbon fixation") (using [hydrogen sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_sulfide "Hydrogen sulfide") as their energy source) and produce sugars and [amino acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amino_acid "Amino acid").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-2)

18**H**2**S** + 6CO 2 + 3**O**2 → C 6**H**12 O 6 ([carbohydrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate "Carbohydrate")) + 12**H**2**O** + 18**S**
Instead of releasing [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen") gas while fixing carbon dioxide as in [photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis "Photosynthesis"), hydrogen sulfide chemosynthesis produces solid globules of [sulfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur "Sulfur") in the process. In bacteria capable of chemoautotrophy (chemosynthesis), such as [purple sulfur bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_sulfur_bacteria "Purple sulfur bacteria"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-3) yellow globules of sulfur are present and visible in the cytoplasm.

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Gollner_Riftia_pachyptila.png/250px-Gollner_Riftia_pachyptila.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gollner_Riftia_pachyptila.png)

 Giant tube worms (_[Riftia pachyptila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riftia\_pachyptila "Riftia pachyptila")_) have an organ containing chemosynthetic bacteria instead of a gut.

In 1890, [Sergei Winogradsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Winogradsky "Sergei Winogradsky") proposed a novel type of life process called "anorgoxydant".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-4) His discovery suggested that some microbes could live solely on inorganic matter and emerged during his physiological research in the 1880s in [Strasbourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strasbourg "Strasbourg") and [Zürich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z%C3%BCrich "Zürich") on sulfur, iron, and nitrogen bacteria.

In 1897, [Wilhelm Pfeffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Pfeffer "Wilhelm Pfeffer") coined the term "chemosynthesis" for the energy production by oxidation of inorganic substances, in association with [autotrophic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autotrophy "Autotrophy") carbon dioxide assimilation—what would be named today as chemolithoautotrophy. Later, the term would be expanded to include also chemoorganoautotrophs, which are organisms that use organic energy substrates in order to assimilate carbon dioxide.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-5) Thus, chemosynthesis can be seen as a synonym of [chemoautotrophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemoautotrophy "Chemoautotrophy").

The term "[chemotrophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemotroph "Chemotroph")", less restrictive, was introduced in the 1940s by [André Lwoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Lwoff "André Lwoff") for the production of energy by the oxidation of electron donors, organic or not, associated with auto- or heterotrophy.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-7)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/BlackSmoker.jpg/250px-BlackSmoker.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BlackSmoker.jpg)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Fauna_on_hydrothermal_vents.jpg/250px-Fauna_on_hydrothermal_vents.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fauna_on_hydrothermal_vents.jpg)

Winogradsky's suggestion was confirmed nearly 90 years later, when hydrothermal [ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean "Ocean") vents were discovered in the 1970s. The hot springs and strange creatures were discovered by _[Alvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DSV\_Alvin "DSV Alvin")_, the world's first deep-sea submersible, in 1977 at the [Galapagos Rift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galapagos_Rift "Galapagos Rift"). At about the same time, then-graduate student [Colleen Cavanaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleen_Cavanaugh "Colleen Cavanaugh") proposed chemosynthetic bacteria that oxidize sulfides or elemental sulfur as a mechanism by which [tube worms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tube_worm_(body_plan) "Tube worm (body plan)") could survive near hydrothermal vents. Cavanaugh later managed to confirm that this was indeed the method by which the worms could thrive, and is generally credited with the discovery of chemosynthesis.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-8)

A 2004 [television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television "Television") series hosted by [Bill Nye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Nye "Bill Nye") named chemosynthesis as one of the 100 greatest scientific discoveries of all time.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-nye-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-10)

In 2013, researchers reported their discovery of bacteria living in the rock of the [oceanic crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_crust "Oceanic crust") below the thick layers of sediment, and apart from the hydrothermal vents that form along the edges of the [tectonic plates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tectonic_plate "Tectonic plate"). Preliminary findings are that these bacteria subsist on the hydrogen produced by chemical reduction of [olivine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivine "Olivine") by seawater circulating in the small veins that permeate the [basalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basalt "Basalt") that comprises oceanic crust. The bacteria synthesize methane by combining hydrogen and carbon dioxide.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-11)

### Chemosynthesis as an innovative area for continuing research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chemosynthesis&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Chemosynthesis as an innovative area for continuing research")]

Despite the fact that the process of chemosynthesis has been known for more than a hundred years, its significance and importance are still relevant today in the transformation of chemical elements in biogeochemical cycles. Today, the vital processes of nitrifying bacteria, which lead to the oxidation of ammonia to nitric acid, require scientific substantiation and additional research. The ability of bacteria to convert inorganic substances into organic ones suggests that chemosynthetics can accumulate valuable resources for human needs.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Chemosynthetic communities in different environments are important biological systems in terms of their ecology, evolution and biogeography, as well as their potential as indicators of the availability of permanent hydrocarbon- based energy sources. In the process of chemosynthesis, bacteria produce organic matter where photosynthesis is impossible. Isolation of thermophilic sulfate-reducing bacteria _Thermodesulfovibrio yellowstonii_ and other types of chemosynthetics provides prospects for further research. Thus, the importance of chemosynthesis remains relevant for use in innovative technologies, conservation of ecosystems, human life in general.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Photosynthesis_en.svg/500px-Photosynthesis_en.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Photosynthesis_en.svg)

Schematic of photosynthesis in plants. The [carbohydrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate "Carbohydrate") produced are stored in or used by the plant.

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Seawifs_global_biosphere.jpg/500px-Seawifs_global_biosphere.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seawifs_global_biosphere.jpg)

Composite image showing the global distribution of photosynthesis, including both oceanic [phytoplankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoplankton "Phytoplankton") and terrestrial [vegetation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetation "Vegetation"). Dark red and blue-green indicate regions of high photosynthetic activity in the ocean and on land, respectively.

**Photosynthesis**[[note 1]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-2) is a [system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_system "Biological system") of [biological processes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_process "Biological process") by which [photopigment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photopigment "Photopigment")-bearing [autotrophic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autotroph "Autotroph")[organisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organism "Organism"), such as most [plants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant "Plant"), [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae "Algae") and [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria"), convert [light energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_energy "Light energy")—typically from [sunlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight "Sunlight")—into the [chemical energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_energy "Chemical energy") necessary to fuel their [metabolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolism "Metabolism"). The term _photosynthesis_ usually refers to **oxygenic photosynthesis**, a process that releases [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen") as a [byproduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byproduct "Byproduct") of [water splitting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_splitting "Water splitting"). Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the [bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_bond "Chemical bond") of intracellular [organic compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_compound "Organic compound") (complex [compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_compound "Chemical compound") containing [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon")), typically [carbohydrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate "Carbohydrate") like [sugars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar "Sugar") (mainly [glucose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucose "Glucose"), [fructose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fructose "Fructose") and [sucrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucrose "Sucrose")), [starches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starch "Starch"), [phytoglycogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoglycogen "Phytoglycogen") and [cellulose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellulose "Cellulose"). When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through [cellular respiration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellular_respiration "Cellular respiration"). Photosynthesis plays a critical role in producing and maintaining the [oxygen content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_oxygen "Atmospheric oxygen") of the [Earth's atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere"), and it supplies most of the [biological energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_energy "Biological energy") necessary for [complex life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_life "Complex life") on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").[[2]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-Bryant-2006-3)

Some organisms also perform [anoxygenic photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anoxygenic_photosynthesis "Anoxygenic photosynthesis"), which does not produce oxygen. Some [bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteria "Bacteria") (e.g. [purple bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_bacteria "Purple bacteria")) use [bacteriochlorophyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteriochlorophyll "Bacteriochlorophyll") to split [hydrogen sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_sulfide "Hydrogen sulfide") as a [reductant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductant "Reductant") instead of [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water"), releasing [sulfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur "Sulfur") instead of oxygen, which was a dominant form of photosynthesis in the [euxinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euxinic "Euxinic")[Canfield oceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canfield_ocean "Canfield ocean") during the [Boring Billion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boring_Billion "Boring Billion").[[3]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-Canfield1998-4)[[4]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-Javaux2018-5)[Archaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaea "Archaea") such as _[Halobacterium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halobacterium "Halobacterium")_ also perform a type of non-[carbon-fixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fixation "Carbon fixation") anoxygenic photosynthesis, where the simpler photopigment [retinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retinal "Retinal") and its [microbial rhodopsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microbial_rhodopsin "Microbial rhodopsin")[derivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative_(chemistry) "Derivative (chemistry)") are used to absorb green light and produce a proton ([hydron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydron "Hydron")) [gradient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrochemical_gradient "Electrochemical gradient") across the [cell membrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_membrane "Cell membrane"), and the subsequent [ion movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemiosmosis "Chemiosmosis") powers [transmembrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transmembrane_protein "Transmembrane protein")[proton pumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton_pump "Proton pump") to directly synthesize [adenosine triphosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adenosine_triphosphate "Adenosine triphosphate") (ATP), the "energy currency" of cells. Such archaeal photosynthesis might have been the earliest form of photosynthesis that evolved on Earth, as far back as the [Paleoarchean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleoarchean "Paleoarchean"), preceding that of [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria") (see [Purple Earth hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Earth_hypothesis "Purple Earth hypothesis")).[[5]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-6)

While the details may differ between [species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species "Species"), the process always begins when light energy is absorbed by the [reaction centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reaction_center "Reaction center"), proteins that contain [photosynthetic pigments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthetic_pigment "Photosynthetic pigment") or [chromophores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromophore "Chromophore"). In plants, these pigments are [chlorophylls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorophyll "Chlorophyll") (a [porphyrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porphyrin "Porphyrin") derivative that absorbs the red and blue [spectra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_spectrum "Optical spectrum") of light, thus reflecting green) held inside [chloroplasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloroplast "Chloroplast"), abundant in [leaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaf "Leaf") cells. In cyanobacteria, they are embedded in the [plasma membrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_membrane "Plasma membrane"). In these [light-dependent reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-dependent_reaction "Light-dependent reaction"), some energy is used to strip [electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron") from suitable substances, such as water, producing oxygen gas. The [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen") freed by the splitting of water is used in the creation of two important molecules that participate in energetic processes: reduced [nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotinamide_adenine_dinucleotide_phosphate "Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate") (NADPH) and ATP.

In plants, [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae "Algae"), and [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria"), sugars are synthesized by a subsequent sequence of light-independent reactions called the [Calvin cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_cycle "Calvin cycle"). In this process, atmospheric carbon dioxide is incorporated into already existing organic compounds, such as [ribulose bisphosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribulose_bisphosphate "Ribulose bisphosphate") (RuBP).[[6]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-7) Using the ATP and NADPH produced by the light-dependent reactions, the resulting compounds are then [reduced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_reductant "Biological reductant") and removed to form further carbohydrates, such as [glucose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucose "Glucose"). In other bacteria, different mechanisms like the [reverse Krebs cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_Krebs_cycle "Reverse Krebs cycle") are used to achieve the same end.

The first photosynthetic organisms probably [evolved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolved "Evolved") early in the [evolutionary history of life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_history_of_life "Evolutionary history of life") using [reducing agents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reducing_agent "Reducing agent") such as hydrogen or hydrogen sulfide, rather than water, as sources of electrons.[[7]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-8) Cyanobacteria appeared later; the [excess oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_cycle "Oxygen cycle") they produced contributed directly to the [oxygenation of the Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygenation_of_the_Earth "Oxygenation of the Earth"),[[8]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-9) which rendered the evolution of complex life possible. The average rate of energy captured by global photosynthesis is approximately 130 [terawatts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terawatts "Terawatts"),[[9]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-10)[[10]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-12) which is about eight times the total [power consumption of human civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_consumption_of_human_civilization "Power consumption of human civilization").[[12]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-13) Photosynthetic organisms also convert around 100–115 billion [tons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ton "Ton") (91–104 Pg [petagrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orders_of_magnitude_(mass) "Orders of magnitude (mass)"), or billions of metric tons), of carbon into [biomass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomass_(ecology) "Biomass (ecology)") per year.[[13]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-McGraw-Hill-2007-15) Photosynthesis was discovered in 1779 by [Jan Ingenhousz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Ingenhousz "Jan Ingenhousz") who showed that plants need light, not just soil and water.

## Overview

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Simple_photosynthesis_overview.svg/250px-Simple_photosynthesis_overview.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Simple_photosynthesis_overview.svg)

Photosynthesis changes sunlight into chemical energy, splits water to liberate O 2, and fixes CO 2 into sugar.

Most photosynthetic organisms are [photoautotrophs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photoautotroph "Photoautotroph"), which means that they are able to [synthesize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_synthesis "Chemical synthesis") food directly from [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") and [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water") using [energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy "Energy") from light. However, not all organisms use carbon dioxide as a source of carbon atoms to carry out photosynthesis; [photoheterotrophs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photoheterotroph "Photoheterotroph") use organic compounds, rather than carbon dioxide, as a source of carbon.[[2]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-Bryant-2006-3)

In [plants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant "Plant"), [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae "Algae"), and [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria"), photosynthesis releases oxygen. This **oxygenic photosynthesis** is by far the most common type of photosynthesis used by living organisms. Some shade-loving plants (sciophytes) produce such low levels of oxygen during photosynthesis that they use all of it themselves instead of releasing it to the atmosphere.[[15]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-16)

Although there are some differences between oxygenic photosynthesis in plants, algae, and cyanobacteria, the overall process is quite similar in these organisms. There are also many varieties of [anoxygenic photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anoxygenic_photosynthesis "Anoxygenic photosynthesis"), used mostly by bacteria, which consume carbon dioxide but do not release oxygen or which produce elemental sulfur instead of molecular oxygen.[[16]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-18)

Carbon dioxide is converted into sugars in a process called [carbon fixation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fixation "Carbon fixation"); photosynthesis captures energy from sunlight to convert carbon dioxide into [carbohydrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate "Carbohydrate"). Carbon fixation is an [endothermic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endothermic "Endothermic")[redox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redox "Redox") reaction.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article is about biological consumption of energy from inorganic compounds. For chemical synthesis in molecular nanotechnology, see [Chemosynthesis (nanotechnology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis_(nanotechnology) "Chemosynthesis (nanotechnology)").

[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Venenivibrio.jpg/250px-Venenivibrio.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Venenivibrio.jpg)

_[Venenivibrio stagnispumantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venenivibrio\_stagnispumantis "Venenivibrio stagnispumantis")_ gains energy by oxidizing hydrogen gas.

In biochemistry, **chemosynthesis** is the biological conversion of one or more carbon-containing molecules (usually [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") or [methane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methane "Methane")) and nutrients into organic matter using the [oxidation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidation "Oxidation") of inorganic compounds (e.g., [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen") gas, [hydrogen sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_sulfide "Hydrogen sulfide")) or [ferrous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrous "Ferrous") ions as a source of energy, rather than sunlight, as in [photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis "Photosynthesis"). [Chemoautotrophs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemotroph "Chemotroph"), [organisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organism "Organism") that obtain carbon from [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") through chemosynthesis, are phylogenetically diverse. Groups that include conspicuous or biogeochemically important taxa include the sulfur-oxidizing [Gammaproteobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammaproteobacteria "Gammaproteobacteria"), the [Campylobacterota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campylobacterota "Campylobacterota"), the [Aquificota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquificota "Aquificota"), the [methanogenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methanogen "Methanogen") archaea, and the neutrophilic [iron-oxidizing bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron-oxidizing_bacteria "Iron-oxidizing bacteria").

Many microorganisms in dark regions of the oceans use chemosynthesis to produce biomass from single-carbon molecules. Two categories can be distinguished. In the rare sites where hydrogen molecules (H 2) are available, the energy available from the reaction between CO 2 and H 2 (leading to production of methane, CH 4) can be large enough to drive the production of biomass. Alternatively, in most oceanic environments, energy for chemosynthesis derives from reactions in which substances such as [hydrogen sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_sulfide "Hydrogen sulfide") or [ammonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia "Ammonia") are oxidized. This may occur with or without the presence of oxygen.

Many chemosynthetic microorganisms are consumed by other organisms in the ocean, and [symbiotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symbiosis "Symbiosis") associations between chemosynthesizers and respiring heterotrophs are quite common. Large populations of animals can be supported by chemosynthetic [secondary production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_production "Secondary production") at [hydrothermal vents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrothermal_vent "Hydrothermal vent"), [methane clathrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methane_clathrate "Methane clathrate"), [cold seeps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_seep "Cold seep"), [whale falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whale_fall "Whale fall"), and [isolated cave water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movile_Cave "Movile Cave").

It has been hypothesized that anaerobic chemosynthesis may support life below the surface of [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_on_Mars "Life on Mars"), [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter")'s moon [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)"), and other planets.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-1) Chemosynthesis may have also been the first type of metabolism that evolved on Earth, leading the way for cellular respiration and photosynthesis to develop later.

## Hydrogen sulfide chemosynthesis process

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chemosynthesis&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Hydrogen sulfide chemosynthesis process")]

[Giant tube worms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_tube_worm "Giant tube worm") use bacteria in their [trophosome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trophosome "Trophosome") to [fix carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fixation "Carbon fixation") (using [hydrogen sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_sulfide "Hydrogen sulfide") as their energy source) and produce sugars and [amino acids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amino_acid "Amino acid").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-2)

18**H**2**S** + 6CO 2 + 3**O**2 → C 6**H**12 O 6 ([carbohydrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate "Carbohydrate")) + 12**H**2**O** + 18**S**
Instead of releasing [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen") gas while fixing carbon dioxide as in [photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis "Photosynthesis"), hydrogen sulfide chemosynthesis produces solid globules of [sulfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur "Sulfur") in the process. In bacteria capable of chemoautotrophy (chemosynthesis), such as [purple sulfur bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_sulfur_bacteria "Purple sulfur bacteria"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-3) yellow globules of sulfur are present and visible in the cytoplasm.

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Gollner_Riftia_pachyptila.png/250px-Gollner_Riftia_pachyptila.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gollner_Riftia_pachyptila.png)

 Giant tube worms (_[Riftia pachyptila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riftia\_pachyptila "Riftia pachyptila")_) have an organ containing chemosynthetic bacteria instead of a gut.

In 1890, [Sergei Winogradsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Winogradsky "Sergei Winogradsky") proposed a novel type of life process called "anorgoxydant".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-4) His discovery suggested that some microbes could live solely on inorganic matter and emerged during his physiological research in the 1880s in [Strasbourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strasbourg "Strasbourg") and [Zürich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z%C3%BCrich "Zürich") on sulfur, iron, and nitrogen bacteria.

In 1897, [Wilhelm Pfeffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Pfeffer "Wilhelm Pfeffer") coined the term "chemosynthesis" for the energy production by oxidation of inorganic substances, in association with [autotrophic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autotrophy "Autotrophy") carbon dioxide assimilation—what would be named today as chemolithoautotrophy. Later, the term would be expanded to include also chemoorganoautotrophs, which are organisms that use organic energy substrates in order to assimilate carbon dioxide.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-5) Thus, chemosynthesis can be seen as a synonym of [chemoautotrophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemoautotrophy "Chemoautotrophy").

The term "[chemotrophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemotroph "Chemotroph")", less restrictive, was introduced in the 1940s by [André Lwoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Lwoff "André Lwoff") for the production of energy by the oxidation of electron donors, organic or not, associated with auto- or heterotrophy.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-7)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/BlackSmoker.jpg/250px-BlackSmoker.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BlackSmoker.jpg)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Fauna_on_hydrothermal_vents.jpg/250px-Fauna_on_hydrothermal_vents.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fauna_on_hydrothermal_vents.jpg)

Winogradsky's suggestion was confirmed nearly 90 years later, when hydrothermal [ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean "Ocean") vents were discovered in the 1970s. The hot springs and strange creatures were discovered by _[Alvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DSV\_Alvin "DSV Alvin")_, the world's first deep-sea submersible, in 1977 at the [Galapagos Rift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galapagos_Rift "Galapagos Rift"). At about the same time, then-graduate student [Colleen Cavanaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleen_Cavanaugh "Colleen Cavanaugh") proposed chemosynthetic bacteria that oxidize sulfides or elemental sulfur as a mechanism by which [tube worms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tube_worm_(body_plan) "Tube worm (body plan)") could survive near hydrothermal vents. Cavanaugh later managed to confirm that this was indeed the method by which the worms could thrive, and is generally credited with the discovery of chemosynthesis.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-8)

A 2004 [television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television "Television") series hosted by [Bill Nye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Nye "Bill Nye") named chemosynthesis as one of the 100 greatest scientific discoveries of all time.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-nye-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-10)

In 2013, researchers reported their discovery of bacteria living in the rock of the [oceanic crust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_crust "Oceanic crust") below the thick layers of sediment, and apart from the hydrothermal vents that form along the edges of the [tectonic plates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tectonic_plate "Tectonic plate"). Preliminary findings are that these bacteria subsist on the hydrogen produced by chemical reduction of [olivine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivine "Olivine") by seawater circulating in the small veins that permeate the [basalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basalt "Basalt") that comprises oceanic crust. The bacteria synthesize methane by combining hydrogen and carbon dioxide.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemosynthesis#cite_note-11)

### Chemosynthesis as an innovative area for continuing research

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chemosynthesis&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Chemosynthesis as an innovative area for continuing research")]

Despite the fact that the process of chemosynthesis has been known for more than a hundred years, its significance and importance are still relevant today in the transformation of chemical elements in biogeochemical cycles. Today, the vital processes of nitrifying bacteria, which lead to the oxidation of ammonia to nitric acid, require scientific substantiation and additional research. The ability of bacteria to convert inorganic substances into organic ones suggests that chemosynthetics can accumulate valuable resources for human needs.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Chemosynthetic communities in different environments are important biological systems in terms of their ecology, evolution and biogeography, as well as their potential as indicators of the availability of permanent hydrocarbon- based energy sources. In the process of chemosynthesis, bacteria produce organic matter where photosynthesis is impossible. Isolation of thermophilic sulfate-reducing bacteria _Thermodesulfovibrio yellowstonii_ and other types of chemosynthetics provides prospects for further research. Thus, the importance of chemosynthesis remains relevant for use in innovative technologies, conservation of ecosystems, human life in general.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Photosynthesis_en.svg/500px-Photosynthesis_en.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Photosynthesis_en.svg)

Schematic of photosynthesis in plants. The [carbohydrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate "Carbohydrate") produced are stored in or used by the plant.

[![Image 2](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Seawifs_global_biosphere.jpg/500px-Seawifs_global_biosphere.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seawifs_global_biosphere.jpg)

Composite image showing the global distribution of photosynthesis, including both oceanic [phytoplankton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoplankton "Phytoplankton") and terrestrial [vegetation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetation "Vegetation"). Dark red and blue-green indicate regions of high photosynthetic activity in the ocean and on land, respectively.

**Photosynthesis**[[note 1]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-2) is a [system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_system "Biological system") of [biological processes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_process "Biological process") by which [photopigment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photopigment "Photopigment")-bearing [autotrophic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autotroph "Autotroph")[organisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organism "Organism"), such as most [plants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant "Plant"), [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae "Algae") and [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria"), convert [light energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_energy "Light energy")—typically from [sunlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight "Sunlight")—into the [chemical energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_energy "Chemical energy") necessary to fuel their [metabolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolism "Metabolism"). The term _photosynthesis_ usually refers to **oxygenic photosynthesis**, a process that releases [oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen "Oxygen") as a [byproduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byproduct "Byproduct") of [water splitting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_splitting "Water splitting"). Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the [bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_bond "Chemical bond") of intracellular [organic compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_compound "Organic compound") (complex [compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_compound "Chemical compound") containing [carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon "Carbon")), typically [carbohydrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate "Carbohydrate") like [sugars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar "Sugar") (mainly [glucose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucose "Glucose"), [fructose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fructose "Fructose") and [sucrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sucrose "Sucrose")), [starches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starch "Starch"), [phytoglycogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytoglycogen "Phytoglycogen") and [cellulose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellulose "Cellulose"). When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through [cellular respiration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellular_respiration "Cellular respiration"). Photosynthesis plays a critical role in producing and maintaining the [oxygen content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_oxygen "Atmospheric oxygen") of the [Earth's atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere"), and it supplies most of the [biological energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_energy "Biological energy") necessary for [complex life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_life "Complex life") on [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth").[[2]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-Bryant-2006-3)

Some organisms also perform [anoxygenic photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anoxygenic_photosynthesis "Anoxygenic photosynthesis"), which does not produce oxygen. Some [bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteria "Bacteria") (e.g. [purple bacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_bacteria "Purple bacteria")) use [bacteriochlorophyll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacteriochlorophyll "Bacteriochlorophyll") to split [hydrogen sulfide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_sulfide "Hydrogen sulfide") as a [reductant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductant "Reductant") instead of [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water"), releasing [sulfur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur "Sulfur") instead of oxygen, which was a dominant form of photosynthesis in the [euxinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euxinic "Euxinic")[Canfield oceans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canfield_ocean "Canfield ocean") during the [Boring Billion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boring_Billion "Boring Billion").[[3]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-Canfield1998-4)[[4]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-Javaux2018-5)[Archaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaea "Archaea") such as _[Halobacterium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halobacterium "Halobacterium")_ also perform a type of non-[carbon-fixing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fixation "Carbon fixation") anoxygenic photosynthesis, where the simpler photopigment [retinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retinal "Retinal") and its [microbial rhodopsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microbial_rhodopsin "Microbial rhodopsin")[derivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative_(chemistry) "Derivative (chemistry)") are used to absorb green light and produce a proton ([hydron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydron "Hydron")) [gradient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrochemical_gradient "Electrochemical gradient") across the [cell membrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_membrane "Cell membrane"), and the subsequent [ion movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemiosmosis "Chemiosmosis") powers [transmembrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transmembrane_protein "Transmembrane protein")[proton pumps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton_pump "Proton pump") to directly synthesize [adenosine triphosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adenosine_triphosphate "Adenosine triphosphate") (ATP), the "energy currency" of cells. Such archaeal photosynthesis might have been the earliest form of photosynthesis that evolved on Earth, as far back as the [Paleoarchean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleoarchean "Paleoarchean"), preceding that of [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria") (see [Purple Earth hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Earth_hypothesis "Purple Earth hypothesis")).[[5]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-6)

While the details may differ between [species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species "Species"), the process always begins when light energy is absorbed by the [reaction centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reaction_center "Reaction center"), proteins that contain [photosynthetic pigments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthetic_pigment "Photosynthetic pigment") or [chromophores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromophore "Chromophore"). In plants, these pigments are [chlorophylls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorophyll "Chlorophyll") (a [porphyrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porphyrin "Porphyrin") derivative that absorbs the red and blue [spectra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_spectrum "Optical spectrum") of light, thus reflecting green) held inside [chloroplasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chloroplast "Chloroplast"), abundant in [leaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaf "Leaf") cells. In cyanobacteria, they are embedded in the [plasma membrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasma_membrane "Plasma membrane"). In these [light-dependent reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-dependent_reaction "Light-dependent reaction"), some energy is used to strip [electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron") from suitable substances, such as water, producing oxygen gas. The [hydrogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen "Hydrogen") freed by the splitting of water is used in the creation of two important molecules that participate in energetic processes: reduced [nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicotinamide_adenine_dinucleotide_phosphate "Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate") (NADPH) and ATP.

In plants, [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae "Algae"), and [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria"), sugars are synthesized by a subsequent sequence of light-independent reactions called the [Calvin cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_cycle "Calvin cycle"). In this process, atmospheric carbon dioxide is incorporated into already existing organic compounds, such as [ribulose bisphosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribulose_bisphosphate "Ribulose bisphosphate") (RuBP).[[6]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-7) Using the ATP and NADPH produced by the light-dependent reactions, the resulting compounds are then [reduced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_reductant "Biological reductant") and removed to form further carbohydrates, such as [glucose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucose "Glucose"). In other bacteria, different mechanisms like the [reverse Krebs cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_Krebs_cycle "Reverse Krebs cycle") are used to achieve the same end.

The first photosynthetic organisms probably [evolved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolved "Evolved") early in the [evolutionary history of life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_history_of_life "Evolutionary history of life") using [reducing agents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reducing_agent "Reducing agent") such as hydrogen or hydrogen sulfide, rather than water, as sources of electrons.[[7]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-8) Cyanobacteria appeared later; the [excess oxygen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_cycle "Oxygen cycle") they produced contributed directly to the [oxygenation of the Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygenation_of_the_Earth "Oxygenation of the Earth"),[[8]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-9) which rendered the evolution of complex life possible. The average rate of energy captured by global photosynthesis is approximately 130 [terawatts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terawatts "Terawatts"),[[9]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-10)[[10]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-12) which is about eight times the total [power consumption of human civilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_consumption_of_human_civilization "Power consumption of human civilization").[[12]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-13) Photosynthetic organisms also convert around 100–115 billion [tons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ton "Ton") (91–104 Pg [petagrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orders_of_magnitude_(mass) "Orders of magnitude (mass)"), or billions of metric tons), of carbon into [biomass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomass_(ecology) "Biomass (ecology)") per year.[[13]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-14)[[14]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-McGraw-Hill-2007-15) Photosynthesis was discovered in 1779 by [Jan Ingenhousz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Ingenhousz "Jan Ingenhousz") who showed that plants need light, not just soil and water.

## Overview

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Simple_photosynthesis_overview.svg/250px-Simple_photosynthesis_overview.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Simple_photosynthesis_overview.svg)

Photosynthesis changes sunlight into chemical energy, splits water to liberate O 2, and fixes CO 2 into sugar.

Most photosynthetic organisms are [photoautotrophs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photoautotroph "Photoautotroph"), which means that they are able to [synthesize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_synthesis "Chemical synthesis") food directly from [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide "Carbon dioxide") and [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water "Water") using [energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy "Energy") from light. However, not all organisms use carbon dioxide as a source of carbon atoms to carry out photosynthesis; [photoheterotrophs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photoheterotroph "Photoheterotroph") use organic compounds, rather than carbon dioxide, as a source of carbon.[[2]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-Bryant-2006-3)

In [plants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant "Plant"), [algae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algae "Algae"), and [cyanobacteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria "Cyanobacteria"), photosynthesis releases oxygen. This **oxygenic photosynthesis** is by far the most common type of photosynthesis used by living organisms. Some shade-loving plants (sciophytes) produce such low levels of oxygen during photosynthesis that they use all of it themselves instead of releasing it to the atmosphere.[[15]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-16)

Although there are some differences between oxygenic photosynthesis in plants, algae, and cyanobacteria, the overall process is quite similar in these organisms. There are also many varieties of [anoxygenic photosynthesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anoxygenic_photosynthesis "Anoxygenic photosynthesis"), used mostly by bacteria, which consume carbon dioxide but do not release oxygen or which produce elemental sulfur instead of molecular oxygen.[[16]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis#cite_note-18)

Carbon dioxide is converted into sugars in a process called [carbon fixation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_fixation "Carbon fixation"); photosynthesis captures energy from sunlight to convert carbon dioxide into [carbohydrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrate "Carbohydrate"). Carbon fixation is an [endothermic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endothermic "Endothermic")[redox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redox "Redox") reaction.
